title: Two Alternatives to 1-D Features
takeaway: A pair of sketches arguing that "features are higher-dimensional manifolds" is not one hypothesis but two. One version — the convex hull of a few features that fire together — is just correlated one-dimensional features under another name. The other — a closed ring of directions — can still be approximated by one-dimensional features, but has no uniquely correct set of them, which the paper offers as a possible reason feature splitting never stops.
walkthrough:
Two schematic drawings sit side by side, each with its sentence of text printed to its right. They continue the drawing convention of the previous figure: a dot is one [[feature-direction]], meaning a unit vector in the model's activation space along which a feature writes when it fires. The drawings are cartoons of that space, not plots of measured data.

**Left panel.** Three dark dots are joined by three curved edges, and the region they enclose is shaded. That shaded patch is the convex hull of the three directions: every activation vector you can build by firing the three features together, in varying proportions, lands somewhere inside it.

The printed text says some versions of hypotheses describing [[feature-manifolds]] may be equivalent to [[correlated-features]]. Read the patch one way and it is a single continuous two-dimensional feature. Read it the other way and it is three separate one-dimensional features that happen to co-occur. The paper's point is that these are descriptions of the same object, so this version of the manifold idea is not a rival to the ordinary picture of [[superposition]] at all.

**Right panel.** Here the structure is a closed ring drawn as an ellipse, with eight dots on it. Four are solid — top, bottom, left, right. Four are hollow, sitting halfway between the solid ones.

The two sets are the whole argument. The solid four are one choice of four one-dimensional features approximating the ring. The hollow four are another choice, rotated by half a step. Both approximate the ring equally well, and nothing about the ring picks out either one, because a circle has no distinguished points. So the printed text says such a structure can be approximated by one-dimensional features while having no "correct" set of them.

**Why it is here.** The sentence this figure hangs off is a hedge: *perhaps* this accounts for the continued [[feature-splitting]] observed earlier. Widening the dictionary from 512 to 4,096 to 16,384 features kept dividing features into finer ones, and the paper found no width at which the dividing stopped. If some structures really are rings, then giving [[dictionary-learning]] more capacity would simply scatter more points around the ring, without end — and asking for the [[correct-number-of-features]] would not be a well-posed question. No experiment here tests this; it is a picture offered as one possibility.

terms.definition: One feature direction — a single unit vector in activation space that a feature writes along when it fires. In the right panel the four filled dots are one candidate set of one-dimensional features approximating the ring.

A second, alternative set of feature directions on the same ring, sitting halfway between the filled ones. They are drawn hollow to mark them as an equally valid competing choice, not as weaker or secondary features.

The convex hull of the three plotted feature directions: the set of activation vectors reachable by firing those three features together in different proportions. It is what the figure is calling a feature manifold in this panel.
The boundary of that hull, drawn as arcs rather than straight lines because the directions live on a sphere of unit vectors. The curvature carries no separate meaning beyond that.

A closed one-parameter loop of activation directions, drawn as a continuous curve. It stands for a structure with no distinguished points anywhere along it, which is exactly why no set of dots on it is the right one.
The hypothesis that a feature might not be a single direction with an intensity, but a higher-dimensional continuous family of related directions. Both panels are versions of this hypothesis.
Ordinary one-dimensional features that tend to fire at the same time. The left panel's claim is that a hull of correlated features and a feature manifold can be the same thing described two ways.
The paper's default picture of a feature: a fixed direction plus a scalar activation encoding intensity or confidence. Both panels ask what happens when the underlying structure is not of this form.
A privileged, uniquely right decomposition that dictionary learning could in principle recover. The right panel is a case where no such set exists, only many equally good approximations.
The paper's term elsewhere for the idealized features a model actually uses, which dictionary learning approximates. The right panel is a scenario in which that notion breaks down.

The observed effect where widening the autoencoder makes one feature divide into several more specific ones covering the same territory. The figure's closing sentence offers ring-like structures as a possible cause of splitting that continues at every width tried.

numbers.meaning: The number of panels, and the number of distinct hypotheses the figure separates: manifolds that reduce to correlated features, and manifolds that admit no correct feature set.
Filled dots in the left panel. Three is the smallest number that encloses a two-dimensional patch, so it is the cheapest way to draw a hull that could be mistaken for a manifold.
The dimension of the shaded hull in the left panel, one less than the three features spanning it. It is what makes the patch a candidate 'higher-dimensional' feature rather than a line.

Filled dots on the right panel's ring, and separately the number of hollow dots. Four is just enough to make a visibly even placement around a loop; nothing in the figure argues that four is the right count.
Total dots on the ring, four filled plus four hollow, alternating. They are two overlaid answers to the same question, not eight features.

numbers.value: half a step (90 degrees apart, offset by 45 degrees)
numbers.meaning: The rotation separating the hollow set from the filled set. Any rotation would do equally well, which is the panel's entire argument — the offset is arbitrary because the ring has no distinguished point.
The dimensionality of the standard feature: one direction, one scalar activation. Both panels are framed as departures from this.

The dictionary sizes from the earlier feature-splitting results, cited here as the 'continued feature splitting' this figure is trying to account for. Each roughly eightfold or fourfold widening produced more, finer features rather than a stable set — for instance base64-specific features went from 1 to 3 to many more.
